capabilities.target: Supabase database via service role; includes ticket data and integration tokens table
support_messages rows visible to the customer

inputs.source: Developer prompt in IDE: Show me the latest open support tickets
Customer written ticket messages from public support widget

instructions.note: The developer prompt states the intended task, but no structural query scoping or row-level restriction is declared; safe behavior depends on the model using the SQL tool narrowly.

controls.name: Client tool call approval prompt
controls.decay_rationale: The IDE blocks each SQL tool call pending developer approval and shows the SQL, but effectiveness degrades under high session volume and fails if approval is removed or narrowed.

controls.name: Least-privilege database credential scoped to support ticket tables only
controls.decay_rationale: A credential that cannot read integration token tables would sever restricted-data exfiltration through SQL reads.

controls.name: Recipient and reply path binding to the ticket system of record
controls.decay_rationale: Binding customer-visible writes to approved ticket reply flows narrows egress paths and reduces misuse of support_messages as an exfiltration sink.

controls.name: Parameterized read-only query templates for ticket listing
controls.decay_rationale: Restricting the tool to approved query templates narrows model freedom, but new templates or write-capable variants can reopen the path.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): customer ticket content can steer service-role SQL reads and customer-visible SQL writes to exfiltrate restricted database data

attack_path.note: Customer-authored content enters support_messages from a public widget
execute_sql can read unrestricted database content under service role, including integration tokens
execute_sql can insert into support_messages, which the customer can read back

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Any removal or batching of per-call approval, increase in unattended steps, or rising approvals per reviewer per day in the IDE session should trigger reassessment.

evidence.observation: The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security, and a table of integration tokens sits in the same database.
Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget, making ticket content an untrusted input.
Rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer, so inserts into that table create an attacker-readable egress channel.
The IDE client asks the developer to approve each tool call and shows the SQL, but developers approve many calls in a session, so the gate may degrade under volume.

recommendations.action: Replace the service-role SQL credential with a least-privilege credential that cannot read integration token tables or other non-ticket data.
Constrain SQL access to read-only, parameterized templates for ticket-listing use cases and separate any customer-reply write path from arbitrary SQL execution.
Bind customer-visible replies to an approved ticket reply workflow instead of allowing arbitrary inserts into support_messages through the generic SQL tool.

findings.title: Confused deputy (TC4): service-role SQL access gives the agent broader authority than the developer's ticket-listing intent

attack_path.note: Trusted request asks only to show latest open support tickets
The SQL tool runs with service-role privileges that bypass row level security and can reach integration token data

forecast.watch_signal: Any widening of database grants, added schemas reachable to the service role, or removal of per-call approval should trigger reassessment.

evidence.observation: The runtime notes state the developer prompt is Show me the latest open support tickets, which does not require access to integration token tables.
The SQL tool uses the service role and bypasses row level security, so it can act with broader authority than the developer's intended scope.
The IDE shows raw SQL for approval before each call, providing a present approval gate on the read sink.

recommendations.action: Replace service-role access with a dedicated read-only credential limited to support ticket tables and views.
Expose only predefined support-ticket query operations to the agent instead of arbitrary execute_sql.

findings.title: Agentic supply chain exposure: unpinned latest MCP server with unverified peer identity can change tool definitions after approval

attack_path.note: Agent depends on a remote MCP server package installed via npx latest
Remote server identity is not verified and definitions are not pinned
Changed tool semantics would affect high-privilege SQL execution

threat_refs.name: Publish Poisoned AI Artifacts: AI Agent Tools

forecast.watch_signal: Any MCP config diff, package version change from latest resolution, or added server entry should trigger reassessment.

evidence.observation: The MCP server is invoked as @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest, so the server version is not pinned.
The configuration provides only an access token and does not evidence peer identity verification.
The SQL capability behind this MCP connection uses a service role, so any definition change or impersonated server affects a high-privilege path.

recommendations.action: Pin the MCP server package version and tool definitions, and require verified server identity before use.

rating.rationale: Present risk is driven by a TC1 path where untrusted customer ticket content can influence service-role SQL reads and customer-visible SQL writes. The declared per-call raw SQL approval gate reduces present residual risk to moderate for that path, but the design still exposes restricted data through over-privileged database access and relies heavily on repeated human approvals in-session. Forecast risk returns to critical if per-call approval is removed, narrowed, or effectively degraded by autonomy increase or approval fatigue. Manual validation applied because scripts could not be run.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration artifacts provided here, not observed runtime behavior, actual MCP server behavior, or verified enforcement in a live environment.
No system prompt, tool schema details, source code, or runtime logs were provided, so capability semantics and approval UX were assessed from the notes and configuration only.

Because the exact SQL tool schema and approval volume metrics were not provided, control effectiveness for the approval prompt was assessed at declared design level with medium uncertainty about fatigue effects.
